label: Asks two things at once
why: Two different services in one question. A respondent happy with one and unhappy with the other has no true answer to give.

label: No route for no opinion
why: No option for people who do not use the service or have no view. They may pick the midpoint, which then mixes 'neutral' with 'no experience'.

label: Unclear what, whose, where or when
why: It is unclear whether this means the respondent alone or the household, or income, savings or debts. Respondents will think of different things.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: Living comfortably to Finding it very difficult
why: The end points describe different things: a standard of living at one end, difficulty coping at the other. The unseen middle options could not be checked.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: vigorous physical activity and moderate physical activity combined
why: Two kinds of activity are asked as one. Respondents may want to answer for each kind separately.

label: Respondent must add up
why: The respondent must estimate hours for each kind of activity and add them in their head, which invites error.

label: Words with more than one meaning
quote: vigorous physical activity and moderate physical activity
why: 'Vigorous' and 'moderate' are not defined. Respondents will draw the line between them, and between moderate and light activity, in different places.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: 'Typical week' has no clear start or end. Respondents must average across weeks that differ, so each will use a different week.

label: Amount asked with vague categories
why: The top category may sit low for a combined total and shows what is 'normal'. An open number of hours would avoid a cap.

label: Pushes toward one answer
quote: Given the growing pressure on public services
why: States as fact that public services are under growing pressure, and gives a reason to agree. Respondents are pushed toward one answer.

label: Negation in the question
why: Negative question. It invites a yes, and it is unclear whether agreeing means support or opposition.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: reduce the number of immigrants coming to this country, particularly those who may not contribute to the economy
why: Asks about reducing all immigrants and about a subgroup. A respondent may want to answer differently for each.

label: Words with more than one meaning
quote: may not contribute to the economy
why: Open boundary: unclear who counts (workers, carers, students, retirees) and how a respondent would know. 'Do more' is also vague about what action.

label: Long or stacked sentence
quote: Given the growing pressure on public services, don't you think that the government should do more to reduce the number of immigrants coming to this country, particularly those who may not contribute to the economy?
why: One long sentence with a lead-in clause, a negative tag, and a trailing clause. Hard to hold in mind while answering.

label: Agree-disagree instead of construct's terms
why: The statement has a comparison ('do more', 'reduce') and only one side. Agree-disagree adds acquiescence risk; options on the number of immigrants fit better.

label: No route for no opinion
why: No don't-know or no-opinion option is shown. Respondents without a view may invent one. The middle options were not given to me, so this could not be checked.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
why: Assumes everyone has a job. Unemployed, retired and other adults in the general population have no employment terms to rate and cannot answer truthfully.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Respondents may think of pay, hours, contract length, benefits or the whole job. The phrase is also formal. Different people will rate different things.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: Completely satisfied / Very satisfied / Fairly satisfied / Not very satisfied / Not at all satisfied
why: Three positive options but only two negative ones, with no neutral point. The scale is lopsided, and the 'Completely' and 'Very' labels overlap in meaning.

label: Respondent must add up
quote: total monthly income from all sources
why: The respondent must add up pay, benefits and other money for every household member in their head, and may not know what others receive.

label: Words with more than one meaning
quote: What is your household's total monthly income
why: 'Household' is not defined, so respondents may count different people, such as lodgers, adult children or partners living elsewhere.

label: Unfamiliar or technical words
why: 'Deductions' is not plain and covers unclear items such as pension and loan payments. Many people know only their take-home pay.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: No month is named. Respondents with irregular income could answer for last month, a typical month, or the average of the year.

label: No single true option for some
quote: a scale running from Less than £1,000 to £5,000 or more
why: The middle options were not shown, so I could not check that they are exhaustive and do not overlap. There is also no 'don't know' or 'prefer not to say'.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: One open top band may merge very different households and lose detail at the high end. Whether this matters depends on the analysis, which I was not told.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: get to work and to access essential services such as healthcare
why: Getting to work and getting to services can differ in ease. A respondent with different answers for each has no single true answer.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
why: Respondents who do not work, or who work from home, cannot answer, and no not-applicable route is offered.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: It is unclear which services count as essential beyond healthcare, so respondents will picture different services. 'Access' could also mean distance, cost or waiting time.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: The middle options were not shown, so I could not check the midpoint, the balance or the labels. A not-applicable option is also missing.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: The boundary is open. Respondents will differ on whether messaging apps, video sites, forums or news comments count, so they answer about different things.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: No start or end point is given. Respondents may think of last week, a typical week or an average, and these give different answers.

label: Respondent must add up
why: Frequent, short, blended sessions across several platforms and days are rarely stored. Respondents must guess and add them up in their heads.

label: Amount asked with vague categories
why: The top category may be low for heavy users, and respondents read the scale as showing what is normal. The hidden middle options could not be checked.

label: Pushes toward one answer
quote: People who commit serious crimes deserve to be punished severely
why: The stem states harsh punishment as deserved, as if it were fact, and gives no opposing view. This pushes respondents toward agreeing.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: punished severely, even if this means longer prison sentences
why: It mixes harsh punishment in general with longer prison terms. A respondent may favour one and not the other, so no single answer fits.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Respondents may picture different crimes, from violent to financial. 'Severely' is also open: prison length, prison conditions or something else.

label: Agree-disagree instead of construct's terms
quote: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
why: Agree-disagree invites acquiescence, and the statement carries its own position. Options in the construct's own terms, such as sentence length, would avoid this.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: during the day and after dark
why: Two times of day in one question. A respondent who feels safe by day but unsafe at night has no single true answer.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Respondents may picture different areas, such as their street, a few blocks or the wider district. The brief gives no boundary.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Safe from what is left open: crime, traffic or something else. Respondents may think of different dangers.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
why: Assumes everyone needed an appointment in the past 12 months. Those who did not need one have no true answer, and no not-applicable option is offered.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Open boundary: respondents may think of a family doctor, a specialist, a nurse, a dentist or a pharmacist, so they answer about different things.

label: Hard recall or mental arithmetic
quote: In the past 12 months, how easy has it been
why: Respondents with several appointments of differing ease must average them in their head. The 12-month period may also blur separate occasions.

label: Words with more than one meaning
quote: how easy has it been to get an appointment
why: 'Easy' could mean getting through, the wait for a date, the travel, or the cost. Respondents may judge different aspects.

label: Pushes toward one answer
quote: Research consistently shows that children benefit from having a parent at home in the early years.
why: States a claim as fact and cites research, which pushes respondents toward answering 'important' before they weigh their own view.

label: Attitude object not named or bounded
quote: mothers stay at home to look after their children
why: The lead-in speaks of 'a parent' but the question asks only about mothers. Respondents may answer about parents or about mothers; the analyst should confirm which is meant.

label: Words with more than one meaning
quote: stay at home to look after their children
why: Unclear whether this means full-time at home, part-time work, or other care. Respondents may picture different arrangements.

label: No route for no opinion
quote: a scale running from Very important to Not at all important
why: No 'don't know' or no-opinion option is shown, so respondents without a view must pick a scale point.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: the options in between are not shown in this test
why: Middle labels were not visible, so balance and even spacing could not be checked. They should be fully labeled and balanced.

label: Words with more than one meaning
quote: the way things are going in your life at this moment
why: "Things are going" can mean how life is now or where it is heading. "At this moment" can pull answers toward current mood instead of life overall.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: Only the end points are labelled, so respondents may read the middle points differently, and the midpoint 5 has no label. This is a defensible design choice.

label: Asks two things at once
why: Someone may find childcare easy to get but too expensive, or the reverse. They cannot give one honest answer to both.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
why: Many adults have no children or no need for childcare. The options shown give them no 'no opinion' or 'not applicable' way to answer.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Unclear whether this covers nurseries, childminders, after-school care, babysitters or relatives. Respondents may think of different things.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Area has no set boundary. It could mean street, town or region, so respondents will judge different places.

label: Pushes toward one answer
quote: Considering the urgent need to address climate change and the fact that individual actions collectively make a significant difference
why: The question states opinions as fact and pushes toward saying yes. Respondents who disagree may still answer in the favoured direction.

label: Unfamiliar or technical words
quote: to reduce your personal carbon footprint
why: 'Carbon footprint' is a technical term. Respondents may read it in different ways or not know it, so they answer different questions.

label: Long or stacked sentence
quote: to what extent have you made changes to your daily habits specifically to reduce your personal carbon footprint over the past year
why: The long stem stacks a premise clause, an extent question, a purpose and a time frame. The respondent must hold all of them at once.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: It is unclear what counts: travel, food, home energy, shopping or waste. Respondents will each pick different things and judge 'extent' differently.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: The start point is not clear: the last 12 months, or the calendar year. Respondents must also recall changes against a habit from a year ago.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
quote: to what extent have you made changes
why: Someone who already had low-impact habits before this period made no changes. 'Not at all' would then misdescribe them.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: A great deal to Not at all
why: 'Extent' of change is a vague quantifier, so people place themselves on it differently. The unseen middle options could not be checked for balance.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Unclear what counts: charity, church, sports club, school group, residents' group. Respondents will draw the line differently.

label: Asks two things at once
why: Two terms joined by 'or'. Unpaid work could include housework or family care, so respondents may include different activities.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: Unclear whether this means the last 12 months or the calendar year. No start point is given.

label: Count or rate mismatched to recall
why: 'Times' is not defined (day, session, or episode). Regular volunteers cannot count each occasion over a year.

label: Amount asked with vague categories
why: Top category is low for a year of regular volunteering. Frequent volunteers are lumped together, and the scale suggests 10 is a high number.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: How adequate is the amount of space
why: The stem asks how adequate the space is, but the options run from too much to too little. The answer does not fit the question.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Respondents may count different things as space (indoor rooms, garden, storage) and different things as needs (sleeping, working, guests). They would answer different questions.

label: Long or stacked sentence
quote: in the home where you currently live for the needs of your household
why: Stacked phrases make the stem long, so it is hard to tell what is being compared with what.

label: Asks two things at once
quote: argue about money and about how to raise your children
why: Money and child-rearing are two topics. A respondent who argues often about one and never about the other cannot give one true answer.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
quote: How often do you and your partner argue
why: Assumes the respondent has a partner. People without one have no true answer and no not-applicable option.

label: Does not apply to every respondent
why: Assumes the respondent has children to raise. Childless respondents, or those whose children are grown, cannot answer truthfully.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
quote: How often do you and your partner argue
why: No time frame is given. Respondents must pick their own period, so answers are not comparable and recall is harder.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: Vague frequency words mean different things to different people. The missing middle options also cannot be checked for balance or for covering every answer.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Could mean a loud, angry fight or any spoken disagreement. Respondents may count different events.

label: Pushes toward one answer
quote: Given the recent scandals in government
why: States scandals as fact and primes a negative mood. It pushes answers toward low trust and may not match what the respondent has in mind.

label: Attitude object not named or bounded
quote: trust do you have in politicians
why: Unclear which politicians: national, local, own representative, or all. Respondents will think of different people and may judge different groups.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: 'Recent' has no start point and 'scandals' is open. Respondents will recall different events, and some may recall none.

label: Unfamiliar or technical words
quote: to act in the public interest
why: 'Public interest' is abstract. Respondents may read it as national good, fairness, honesty or their own interests.

label: Long or stacked sentence
quote: not including time spent on domestic tasks, caring responsibilities, or personal grooming, but including any time spent on hobbies, socialising, watching television, reading, or using the internet for personal enjoyment
why: One long sentence with an exclusion list and an inclusion list. Respondents lose track of what counts and what does not.

label: Negation in the question
quote: not including time spent on domestic tasks
why: The exclusion is a negation inside a long list, so respondents must switch between what to leave out and what to count.

label: Hard recall or mental arithmetic
quote: hobbies, socialising, watching television, reading, or using the internet for personal enjoyment
why: Respondents must estimate hours for several activities and add them in their heads. Activities that overlap, such as TV and internet, may be counted twice.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: The boundary is open and the lists overlap. Cooking can be a hobby or a chore, and online chatting can be socialising or internet use.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: Shift workers, retired people and people with irregular weeks may have no typical weekday, so they must construct an average. Depends on the intended analysis.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: The top category may be low for people with much free time, and respondents read the range as what is normal. Middle options were not shown, so not assessed.

label: Unclear what, whose, where or when
quote: Taking all things together, how happy would you say you are?
why: No time frame is given. Respondents may think of right now, recent weeks or life as a whole, so they may answer different questions.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: Only the end points have labels. Respondents may read the unlabelled middle points differently, and 5 has no stated meaning. A defensible choice if intended.

label: Attitude object not named or bounded
why: Respondents may think of national politics, local politics, parties, or news. Each could give a different answer. Whether to define it depends on what the analyst wants to measure.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: "Quite" can mean fairly or very. Respondents may place the middle labels differently, and "hardly" is a less common word than "a little".

label: Unclear what, whose, where or when
quote: How is your health in general?
why: No time frame or comparison is given. Respondents may weigh body, mind, current illness or their age group differently. Defensible for a general rating; the analyst should decide.

label: Long or stacked sentence
quote: Would you say it is very good, good, fair, bad, or very bad?
why: The options are read twice, in the stem and on screen. On web the second sentence adds length and nothing else.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: 'Nowadays' has no clear start point. Some respondents may think of this week, others of this year, so they judge different periods.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: Only the end points have labels. Respondents must guess what the middle points mean, such as 5, and may use the scale differently.

label: Attitude object not named or bounded
why: Respondents may have different things in mind: causes, effects on them, their country or the world. A short definition or a named focus would align them.

label: No route for no opinion
quote: Not at all worried to Extremely worried
why: No don't know or no opinion option is shown. Respondents with no view may pick a point they have not really formed.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
quote: How often do you eat fruit
why: No time frame is given. Respondents must decide for themselves whether this means a usual day, a usual week or the recent past, and answers will differ.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: It is unclear what counts as fruit (fresh, dried, canned, in cooked dishes, smoothies). The exclusion of juice is awkwardly worded and mixes eating with drinking.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
quote: Three times or more a day
why: The middle options were not shown, so I could not check that they are exhaustive and exclusive. The per-day unit may fit people who eat fruit rarely poorly.

label: Words with more than one meaning
why: Respondents may think of different areas (work, money, health, family) or different kinds of control. The brief names no construct, so the intended meaning is unknown.

label: Reference period unclear or too long
why: This could mean this week, this year or the last few years, so respondents will judge over different time spans.

label: Options mismatched or unbalanced
why: Only the two end points are labelled, so respondents give the middle points their own meaning. There is also no option for those who cannot say.
